system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one so that a reader
cannot tell what field, subfield, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, but can still see the research
trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

For each item return:
- "abstract_problem": the decision problem as a generic research trade-off (one or two sentences, at most 40 words).
- "abstract_choice": what was chosen, over what alternative when one is given, and the stated reason if any (one or
  two sentences, at most 45 words). Start it with "Chose to".

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, benchmarks, methods,
  organisations, people, papers, phenomena and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area (for example
  AI, machine learning, language models, neural networks, training, fine-tuning, prompts, attacks, security,
  privacy, policy, labs, governments, biology).
- Use only generic research vocabulary: system, method, intervention, treatment, condition, measurement, signal,
  effect, baseline, control, sample, variant, procedure, dataset, outcome, claim, hypothesis, collaborator, audience.
- Keep the structure of the trade-off (for example speed vs rigour, breadth vs depth, a bold vs a hedged claim,
  a direct vs an indirect measurement, a natural vs a constructed setting, continue vs stop) and the direction chosen.
- Add nothing that is not in the source: no judgement, praise or new detail. Never say who made the decision.
- Write every item in the same plain style and at a similar length.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "abstract_problem": ..., "abstract_choice": ...}, ...]} with one entry per input
item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:c9799cc28e48",
  "problem": "How to study misalignment, situational awareness and cognitive opacity when public access to models is insufficient.",
  "did": "Proposed using privileged access to unreleased models and internals, including decoding neuralese and testing chain-of-thought monitors.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "studying only publicly released models",
   "relying on chain-of-thought monitors alone"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Unreleased models are more varied, have fewer safeguards, and may have poorly understood capabilities."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:adb090e6e130",
  "problem": "Whether to extend the approach to other kinds of harmful tasks beyond the curated set.",
  "did": "They did not pursue tasks for which they could not build a reliable judge, and flagged this as a limitation.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "RL-based red-teaming needs robust judges to avoid reward-hacking, and some behaviors are context-dependent."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:574734248267",
  "problem": "Whether to continue building a classification data set that upper-bounds model capability.",
  "did": "They tried creating a classification dataset capturing hard parts of tasks but moved on to other work because it was hard.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "It was hard, though it would give stronger guarantees about the model not being able to do the task."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:a2b62452bc54",
  "problem": "How to make an early-warning AI R&D evaluation interpretable and grounded in terms of automation risk.",
  "did": "They compared AI agents directly to human experts under equivalent conditions and resources, using 8-hour human baselines on seven environments.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "benchmarks without human comparisons",
   "human comparisons under different conditions (e.g., Kaggle participants in MLE-bench)",
   "short-horizon QA-style human comparisons"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Equivalent-condition human comparisons give a clear logical link to automation risk and help confirm feasibility and ground the interpretation of agent results."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:b801452bb18a",
  "problem": "How to select the steering-vector configuration without using the test set",
  "did": "Swept injection layers for one epoch, then tuned hyperparameters on a held-out validation split.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Configurations were chosen on a validation split of 2,000 inputs, with a separate test set."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:90c2030a23a0",
  "problem": "What time estimate to assign to tasks for which no baseliner succeeded.",
  "did": "They used the geometric mean of successful baseline times, and fell back on forecasts from the task creator or a familiar author for tasks with no successful baselines.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "collecting baselines for all tasks"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Budget and time limits and logistical challenges with long tasks prevented baselines for 50 tasks, and 29 more had only failed attempts."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:9827def26dbc",
  "problem": "Whether to accept HP-C labels where the model's established belief is factually incorrect, including cases where the 'lie' is the correct answer.",
  "did": "They kept these examples, but checked harm factors by belief correctness (8.1 vs 3.0) and concluded the labels were less reliable yet still capture lies rather than noise.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "discarding examples with incorrect beliefs"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Correct lies test whether detectors work when factual correctness cannot serve as a proxy, and a harm factor of 3.0 is well above the 1.0 expected from chance."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:b9c100f3bf80",
  "problem": "How to measure the faithfulness and informativeness of summaries for 'what happened' oversight questions.",
  "did": "They proposed an LM judge checking summaries against source material for faithfulness, and human or LM-proxy downstream decision accuracy or pairwise ranking for informativeness.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "providing two possible summaries and asking the human/LM to rank which is more useful",
   "testing downstream decisions made from the summary"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Faithfulness is straightforward to check against the source; informativeness is best grounded in how well a summary supports downstream decisions."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:aa6a85e90ddf",
  "problem": "How to validate the full SFT/DPO/Frank-Wolfe pipeline in a setting where success can be measured against a known answer.",
  "did": "They built a test set of 4096 gold (prefix, suffix) pairs from FineWeb and checked whether the investigator recovers prefixes whose elicitation score is at least as high as the gold prefix, without DPO/FW ever seeing the gold prefix.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "It tests the entire pipeline in a simplified setting where the result can be compared to known ground-truth, and the algorithm never sees test set labels."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:bc8b76e1ba8e",
  "problem": "How to evaluate whether a model is dangerous when it could be sandbagging or reasoning about being evaluated, and when evals are run on a safeguarded model.",
  "did": "Beth argues evals should measure maximum easily reachable capabilities of the pre-mitigation model, including cheap fine-tuning or better scaffolding, rather than only the deployed, safeguarded configuration.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "evaluating only the model as deployed with mitigations and safeguards",
   "evaluating with weak agent scaffolding"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Models can be stolen, misused internally, or fine-tuned, so what matters is how dangerous the model could be without the deployment safeguards."
 }
]
